theory.intro: The **multiplicity** of a zero decides how the curve meets the $x$-axis there. An odd multiplicity crosses the axis and an even multiplicity turns back without crossing. A multiplicity of $3$ or more flattens the curve against the axis.
facts: At a zero of multiplicity $1$ the curve cuts the $x$-axis at an angle, like a straight line.
At a zero of even multiplicity the curve is tangent to the $x$-axis and bounces back, like a parabola.
At a zero of odd multiplicity $3$ or more the curve has a horizontal point of inflection on the axis and crosses.
Every zero of multiplicity $2$ or more is a stationary point, because $P'$ is zero there as well.
A zero of multiplicity $m$ counts $m$ times towards the degree, so the multiplicities add to the degree.
steps: Write $P(x)$ in factored form and read the multiplicity of each zero.
If the multiplicity is $1$, the curve cuts straight through the $x$-axis.
If the multiplicity is even, the curve touches the $x$-axis and turns back.
If the multiplicity is odd and at least $3$, the curve flattens along the axis as it crosses.

foundation.question_text: Describe the behaviour of the graph of $y=(x-2)^{2}(x+1)$ at each of its $x$-intercepts.
Describe the behaviour of the graph of $y=x(x-2)^{3}$ at each of its $x$-intercepts.
Describe the behaviour of the graph of $y=(x+2)^{2}(x-1)^{2}$ at each of its $x$-intercepts.

foundation.solution_text:
At $x=0$ the curve touches the axis and turns back, so the multiplicity is even, and the smallest even value is $2$.
At $x=3$ the curve cuts straight through, so the multiplicity is $1$.
$2+1=3$, which matches the degree of a cubic.

The curve flattens along the $x$-axis at $x=1$ and crosses, so the multiplicity is odd and at least $3$.
The multiplicities add to the degree $3$, and $x=1$ is the only zero, so its multiplicity is $3$.

foundation.question_text: Describe the behaviour of the graph of $y=-(x+1)^{2}(x-4)$ at each of its $x$-intercepts, and state what happens as $x\to\infty$.

development.question_text: Describe the behaviour of the graph of $y=x(x-1)^{2}(x+2)$ at each of its $x$-intercepts.

development.solution_text:
At $x=-2$ the curve flattens along the axis and crosses, so the multiplicity is odd and at least $3$.
At $x=1$ the curve cuts straight through, so that zero has multiplicity $1$.
The multiplicities add to the degree $4$, so the multiplicity at $x=-2$ is $3$.

Touching at $x=-2$ needs an even multiplicity, so the least is $2$.
Flattening while crossing at $x=1$ needs an odd multiplicity of at least $3$, so the least is $3$.
$2+3=5$, so the least possible degree is $5$.
A possible equation is $y=(x+2)^{2}(x-1)^{3}$.

development.question_text: Describe the behaviour of the graph of $y=(2x-3)^{2}(x+1)$ at each of its $x$-intercepts.
Describe the behaviour of the graph of $y=-(x+1)^{2}(x-3)^{2}$ at each of its $x$-intercepts, and state the sign of $y$ elsewhere.

mastery.solution_text:
Flattening while crossing at $x=-1$ means an odd multiplicity of at least $3$.
With a simple zero at $x=2$ the multiplicities are $3$ and $1$, which add to the degree $4$.
$y=k(x+1)^{3}(x-2)$
$-2=k(1)^{3}(-2)$
$-2=-2k$
$k=1$
$y=(x+1)^{3}(x-2)$

mastery.question_text: For $y=(x-1)^{2}(x+1)^{3}$, describe the behaviour at each $x$-intercept, state the degree, and describe the behaviour as $x\to\infty$ and as $x\to-\infty$.
mastery.solution_text:
$x=1$ has multiplicity $2$, so the curve touches the $x$-axis at $(1,0)$ and turns back.
$x=-1$ has multiplicity $3$, so the curve flattens along the axis at $(-1,0)$ and crosses.
$2+3=5$, so the degree is $5$.
The degree is odd and the leading coefficient is positive, so $y\to\infty$ as $x\to\infty$ and $y\to-\infty$ as $x\to-\infty$.

\begin{axis}[axis lines=middle, xlabel={$x$}, ylabel={$y$}, xmin=-2.4, xmax=2.2, ymin=-10.5, ymax=12.5, samples=120, clip=false, width=9cm, height=8cm]
\addplot[smooth, thick, <->, domain=-2.03:1.76] {(x-1)*(x-1)*(x+1)*(x+1)*(x+1)};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

Touching at $x=1$ gives an even multiplicity and flattening while crossing at $x=-2$ gives an odd multiplicity of at least $3$.
The multiplicities add to $5$, so they are $2$ and $3$.
$y=k(x-1)^{2}(x+2)^{3}$
$8=k(-2)^{2}(1)^{3}$
$8=4k$
$k=2$
$y=2(x-1)^{2}(x+2)^{3}$
